articles.title: ‘Terrorist’ groups in Syria hit after Jordan church attack
articles.description: AMMAN — Jordan’s military said it had struck “terrorist organizations” in neighboring Syria on Monday in retaliation for a deadly jihadist attack on a church last week, hours after authorities arrested three men they accused of the killings. The military said air force jets had “destroyed several terrorist positions” and killed and wounded “numerous members” of groups linked to the perpetrators of the church attack. Syrian authorities reported civilian casualties from the raids, with health officials in southern Daraa province saying six people, including three children and a woman, were killed. Syria’s civil defense agency reported seven deaths in total, six people in Daraa and one in neighboring Sweida province. On Friday, gunmen killed nine people during a funeral service at the Greek Orthodox Saint George’s Church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate, southern Jordan. Karak is home to a significant Christian community in Muslim-majority Jordan, where Christians make up between 2 and 3 percent of the population. Maj. Gen. Abdullah al-Maaytah, Jordan’s director of public security, on Monday named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein. The trio — two of them brothers and the other related by marriage — were cornered at an abandoned house where they had barricaded themselves inside and opened fire on security forces. “All three terrorists have been injured. They have been taken to [the] hospital and are still receiving treatment,” Maaytah told a press conference. ‘We will show them’ One of the suspects was in critical condition, Jordan’s state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka reported. There were no casualties among the security forces, it added. “This country must remain an oasis of security and stability, and we affirm that Jordan will remain impervious to anyone who dares to challenge it,” Maaytah said. Under Jordanian law, murder is punishable by death by hanging. A number of weapons and a large quantity of ammunition were seized from the three suspects, the Public Security Directorate said. Jordan’s King Abdullah II said in a post on X that security forces “chased them to the very end.” “We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote. Earlier, the king visited wounded victims of the church attack in the hospital, dressed in military fatigues and carrying a pistol on his hip. “We will show them,” he vowed. Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al-Mamlaka on Monday that the attackers were all Jordanians and “had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack.” “There is no indication of any external contacts or collaboration with foreign parties,” he said. Government communications chief Mohammad al-Momani said “we stand ready and will strike with an iron fist, without mercy or leniency, against anyone who attempts to undermine Jordan’s security.” Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare. In 2016, an attack in Karak targeted a security center and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead. On Friday, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning for the victims of the church attack, with flags to be flown at half-staff over government and public institutions. Eight of the nine victims were laid to rest on Sunday next to the church in a funeral that drew a huge crowd amid a large security presence, AFP images showed. The ninth person, Mohammed al-Qasous, was buried in south Amman on Monday.

articles.title: Jordan Bombs 'Militant Camp' In Southern Syria After Church Attack, High Death Toll
articles.description: Jordan Bombs 'Militant Camp' In Southern Syria After Church Attack, High Death Toll Jordan's response to the last Friday terror attack on an Orthodox Church in Hammoud, Karak - south of the capital Amman - has been somewhat unexpected. On Monday the country's air force carried out a major bombing raid on southern Syria. There were three gunmen that had targeted St. George church during a funeral. The attackers killed at least eight people and wounded around 40 more. Jordan's King Abdullah had ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" amid the hunt for the killers. Since then, the government announced it arrested the trio of suspects, including two brothers and their brother-in-law, after a shootout at what was described as their hideout. But in addition to the arrests, "Jordan said on Tuesday it had killed more than 20 Daesh militants in airstrikes on southern Syria the previous evening, launched in response to a deadly church attack in Jordan that authorities linked to militants operating across the border," according to Reuters. But the Syrian side, which has strongly condemned the incursion and violation of sovereignty, indicated that "the strikes killed seven people, including three children and a woman. Jordan regretted the civilian casualties, Government Communication Minister Mohammed al-Momani said in a post on X." Amman further said that the target of the air raid was a 'militant hideout' and that the suspects in the church attack were linked to "terrorist groups" based there. The Jordanian government has elsewhere described that targeted group as members of ISIS, and offered a far higher death toll than the Syrian side, saying that "more than 20 Islamic State militants" were taken out. On the prior terror assault of the church last week, Priest Theodoros Soueiss described that "A sense of panic took hold among those present. The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land." Reported scenes of the night time bombing of southern Syria: That among the first actions taken by the Jordanian government was to bomb southern Syria is deeply ironic and hypocritical considering the recent history of conflict and Amman's role. For years during the prior Syrian proxy war, Jordan played host to CIA and Pentagon training programs for anti-Assad militants, most which turned out to be jihadists. This in turned fueled the persecution of the region's ancient Christian community. Tyler Durden Tue, 10/27/2026 - 09:00

articles.title: Jordan attacks militant groups in Syria in retaliation for church attack
articles.description: AMMAN — Jordan has carried out airstrikes against what its military says were terrorist groups in Syria in retaliation for Friday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the southern governorate of Karak that killed nine people. Jordanian air force said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not name the groups or the precise location of the strikes. Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man. Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria said it had not been notified of Monday's attack. Damascus said it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas. In response to the strike, Syria said it had closed a border crossing with Jordan."The decision includes the complete suspension of passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, to ensure the safety of travellers and workers at the crossing," Syrian authorities said in a statement carried by state media. It added that it had "opened direct channels of communication" with Jordanian officials and had launched "comprehensive investigations to establish the full circumstances of the targeting".Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law over the church attack. The Public Security Directorate said the unnamed "terrorists" were found hiding in an abandoned house in Karak before dawn. Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told state-affiliated TV the attackers were all Jordanians and "had been holed up in a building in one of the villages near the site of the attack".
